questions.q: About how many steps does fast exponentiation need for an exponent of 10^18?
questions.e: Each step halves the exponent, so it takes about log₂(10^18) ≈ 60 steps.

questions.q: 13 = 1101 in binary. Which product equals a¹³?
questions.e: The 1-bits of 1101 are worth 8, 4 and 1, so a¹³ = a⁸ × a⁴ × a¹. The loop multiplies in exactly those squared powers.

questions.q: Why reduce the base with a %= m before the loop?
o: It makes the loop run fewer times
So that a × a can't overflow
It is needed only for negative numbers
questions.e: After a %= m, every product is below m², which fits in a long long. A huge base like 10^18 would overflow on the first squaring.
It computes 2¹⁰ mod 10: 2¹⁰ = 1024, whose last digit is 4.

questions.q: p is prime and b isn't a multiple of p. The inverse of b mod p is:
questions.e: Fermat's little theorem says b^(p−1) ≡ 1, so b × b^(p−2) ≡ 1. That makes b^(p−2) the inverse.

questions.q: What is the time complexity of fast exponentiation for exponent b?
questions.e: The exponent is halved every step, so the loop runs about log₂ b times.

questions.q: Why not use pow() from <cmath> to compute aᵇ mod 10⁹ + 7?
o: pow() is too slow for small numbers
pow() works with double: it loses digits and can't take a modulus
questions.e: pow() returns a double. Big results lose their exact digits, and there's no way to take a modulus in the middle.
